opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when we were building MXNet, a lot of the work was really about making things run fast on different hardware. At that time, the main target was NVIDIA GPUs, and we relied heavily on libraries like cuDNN. But every time a new operator came out, or someone wanted to run on a different device, a phone, an ARM CPU, or some new accelerator, we had to go back and hand-write and hand-tune kernels again. It was a huge amount of engineering effort, and it didn't scale. You have a growing number of models and operators on one side and a growing number of hardware backends on the other, and you end up with this M-times-N problem where people are writing optimized code for every combination.

At some point I started asking myself, is there a more systematic way to do this? Instead of humans writing every kernel by hand, can we have a layer that takes a high-level description of the computation and automatically generates efficient code for different hardware? That's essentially a compiler problem. I was also inspired by work like Halide from the image processing community, which separated the description of the computation from how it's scheduled.

So that line of thinking led to TVM. The idea was to build an end-to-end deep learning compiler stack, and later we added machine learning-based approaches like AutoTVM, using learning to search for good optimizations instead of relying entirely on human experts. Looking back, it felt like a natural progression. Building the framework showed me where the real bottleneck was, and the bottleneck was really about how we map computation onto hardware efficiently. That's what pulled me into compilers.

r001.rationale: The response says MXNet required repeated hand-written, hand-tuned kernels across operators and hardware, which did not scale, and describes compiler code generation as a way to reduce that human engineering effort.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So with MXNet, one of the things I learned very quickly is how much of the work in a deep learning framework isn't the algorithms at all. It's the operators. Every time someone wanted a new layer, or a new hardware target, or a slightly different data layout, somebody had to sit down and hand-write a kernel for it. And then write it again for the GPU. And then tune it for a different GPU. And then do the same thing when a mobile chip or an FPGA showed up.

At some point I did a rough count of what fraction of the framework's effort was going into that kind of operator engineering, and it was most of it. We had a small team, and the hardware landscape was expanding faster than we could possibly keep up by hand. That felt fundamentally unsustainable. You're essentially doing an M times N problem: M operators, N backends, and the matrix just keeps growing.

That's when I started thinking about it less as a systems-engineering problem and more as a compiler problem. If you can describe the computation at a high level, separate what you want to compute from how it gets scheduled on a particular piece of hardware, then you can generate those kernels instead of writing them. That idea was already there in Halide for image processing, and it seemed like deep learning workloads were an even better fit, because they're so regular.

So TVM really came directly out of that pain. It was partly frustration, honestly, and partly the realization that the only way a small group could support the whole hardware ecosystem was to automate the thing we'd been doing by hand. Once you make that shift, you also start asking whether machine learning itself can help pick the schedules, and that opened a whole other direction. But the starting point was really just: we cannot keep writing these kernels forever.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the hardware landscape was too large for MXNet’s small team to support by hand and that automation was the only way a small group could support the ecosystem.

astra-6.text:
Working on MXNet, I saw how much engineering went into making each operator run efficiently across different hardware. You could implement an operation for a CPU, then need another implementation for a GPU, and keep tuning those implementations as models and hardware changed. A lot of that work was manual, and it was difficult to scale.

That made me interested in whether we could capture more of that engineering knowledge in a compiler. If we describe the computation at a higher level, can the system generate an efficient implementation for a particular piece of hardware, rather than requiring someone to write and optimize every kernel? For me, compilers became a way to address a very practical problem we were encountering in building and supporting a deep learning framework.

r001.rationale: The response says compiler generation could reduce manual kernel-writing work and make the effort scale, but it does not clearly state that the goal was to support MXNet with fewer engineers.

sol-6.1.text:
Working on MXNet, I saw how much engineering effort went into making operators run efficiently on different hardware. You could get one implementation working well, but then a new device or a new model would come along, and you would have to do a lot of that work again. Maintaining all those specialized implementations became a real challenge.

That made me interested in whether we could automate more of the process. Instead of manually writing and tuning every kernel, could we describe the computation and have a compiler generate an efficient implementation for the hardware? For me, compilers became a way to make that engineering effort more reusable, so supporting new models and new hardware wouldn’t always require starting over.

r001.rationale: The response says compilers could automate and reuse engineering work, reducing repeated effort to support new models and hardware. It does not say this would let MXNet or similar systems be supported with fewer engineers.
